table.title: Mixed · Multilingual glossary
table.md:
| English | 中文 | 日本語 | 한국어 | العربية |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Table | 表格 | 表 | 표 | جدول |
| Line break | 换行 | 改行 | 줄 바꿈 | فاصل الأسطر |
| Readability | 可读性 | 可読性 | 가독성 | سهولة القراءة |
| Horizontal scrolling | 横向滚动 | 横スクロール | 가로 스크롤 | التمرير الأفقي |
| Column width allocation | 列宽分配 | 列幅の割り当て | 열 너비 할당 | توزيع عرض الأعمدة |

understanding.purpose: Provide equivalent glossary terms across five languages.
understanding.reading: Readers find a term in one language and scan across its row to compare translations; consistent row alignment helps them keep their place.
groups: All five columns serve the same role as language equivalents; English can also act as an entry point for readers of this English-language table.
Chinese, Japanese, and Korean terms are compact and can share the middle of the table without requiring identical widths.
keep_intact: Individual English and Arabic words and all language names.
Short glossary terms where space permits, especially compact Chinese, Japanese, and Korean entries.
may_wrap: Multiword English and Arabic terms can wrap between words.
Longer Japanese and Korean terms may wrap at natural script-appropriate boundaries; wrapping can share row height with translations that already need multiple lines.

preferred.name: r2B
preferred.note: Give Japanese its full 93px one-line requirement while keeping the longest Chinese and Korean terms intact. English and Arabic share the remaining space, so their multiword terms may wrap more.

acceptable.name: r1B
acceptable.note: Give Japanese more room and fit the longest Chinese term on one line, while retaining a moderate Arabic column. This tests whether fewer Japanese breaks improve the row rhythm enough to justify a narrower Korean column.

acceptable.name: r1C
acceptable.note: Give English more prominence than in r0B while retaining substantially more Arabic space than r0A. This tests a reader path that starts in English, with wrapping shared across the longer translations.

acceptable.name: r2A
acceptable.note: Refine r1A by giving Japanese 5px more while retaining enough width for the longest Chinese and Korean terms. Arabic gives up 5px; check whether its wrapping remains comfortable.

acceptable.name: r3A
acceptable.note: Keep r2B’s English and Japanese widths, and give Arabic 10px more by reducing Chinese and Korean by 5px each. This tests whether a wider Arabic column improves the lower rows while keeping the compact middle-language terms readable.

acceptable.name: r3B
acceptable.note: Give English the breathing room of r2A while retaining more width for Arabic than r2A and more for Japanese than r2C. This tests a compromise between English prominence and intact translations.

acceptable.name: r3C
acceptable.note: Prioritize the full Japanese term, Korean’s one-line width, and more space for Arabic. The narrower English column may add a wrap, but its individual words still fit; this tests whether keeping more translations intact improves cross-row scanning.

bad.name: r2C
bad.note: Keep r1C's wider English entry point but restore enough width for the longest Chinese and Korean terms. This tests whether a narrower Arabic column produces acceptable wrapping.
bad.why: The narrow Arabic column wraps several short entries, making otherwise compact rows taller and leaving conspicuous empty space across the other languages.

rationale: r2B gives the Chinese, Japanese and Korean entries enough room to remain intact, while the English and Arabic columns accommodate their longer terms with only the necessary wrapping. The last two rows remain easy to scan across, and the columns retain distinct widths suited to their scripts and content.

general: Allocate width according to how content wraps and how readers compare columns, rather than making columns equal by default.
A wrap is less disruptive when it occurs in a row that already needs extra height and preserves recognizable words or phrases.
specific: Japanese benefits from enough width to keep its longest entry on one line; Chinese reaches that point with substantially less space.
Arabic needs more width than r2C provides to keep the shorter entries on one line.

tradeoffs: A designer might prefer more room for English or Arabic at the expense of wrapping in one of the East Asian columns, especially if readers are expected to scan one language more closely.
uncertain: The ranges are conservative estimates around r2B, with other columns adjusted proportionally to remain within the width limit. Intermediate widths were not rendered, so their visual equivalence and exact wrap thresholds are unverified.

critique.good: English has a generous entry column, and the Japanese header and shorter terms sit comfortably. All headers and individual words remain intact.
critique.problems: The Arabic translations wrap repeatedly, making four rows tall and pulling attention toward the narrow right edge. Chinese and Korean also wrap in the longer rows.
critique.cause: English receives 160px, while Arabic receives only 79px, Chinese 65px, and Korean 75px. The extra English width does not prevent its longest phrase from wrapping, but the restricted translation columns create additional lines.

critique.good: The first three data rows are compact, Arabic has a more comfortable measure, and the table has a clear left-to-right rhythm. Words and headers remain intact.
critique.problems: Chinese and Korean break the horizontal-scrolling term across lines, and the last row wraps in several columns. The narrow Chinese column looks crowded beside the more generous Japanese and Arabic columns.
critique.cause: Chinese has 70px and Korean 75px, leaving 49px and 54px for text. Both fall short of their respective longest one-line content widths.

critique.good: Arabic terms fit comfortably, Korean has useful space, and the table remains compact. The first three data rows are easy to scan.
critique.problems: Japanese wraps the horizontal-scrolling term, while Chinese wraps in both longer rows. English is tight for the table's likely entry point, and the Arabic column appears disproportionately spacious.
critique.cause: Japanese and Chinese have only 69px and 44px of text space, respectively, while Arabic has 103px, slightly more than its longest one-line content needs. English has 89px of text space.

critique.good: The columns have a balanced rhythm, the headers remain intact, and the compact Chinese and Korean terms stay on one line. The two taller rows are easy to follow across the table.
critique.problems: The longest Japanese term wraps, as do the two longest English terms and the longest Arabic term. The final row has several short lines, making it feel busier than the rows above.
critique.cause: The Japanese column provides 79px of text space against a 93px one-line requirement. English and Arabic provide 104px and 73px respectively, less than their longest one-line terms require.

critique.good: The wider Japanese and Arabic columns give those translations more room, while the headers and English words remain intact.
critique.problems: Korean terms wrap in both of the taller rows, creating narrow fragments. Japanese still wraps in the final row, so the extra width there has not kept its longest term together.
critique.cause: The 75px Korean column provides only 54px of text space, below the 64px needed for its longest term. The 110px Japanese column provides 89px, just short of the 93px needed.

critique.good: The wider English column gives the English entries a more comfortable measure, and the Arabic column is slightly more generous than in r1A.
critique.problems: Chinese and Korean both break into short fragments in the longer rows, while Japanese also wraps in the final row. This makes the middle of the table look crowded and weakens the horizontal reading rhythm.
critique.cause: The 70px Chinese and 75px Korean columns provide 49px and 54px of text space, below their respective 54px and 64px one-line requirements. The 100px Japanese column also falls short of its longest term.

critique.good: The headers are clear, the first three entries remain compact, and the final two rows have enough height to accommodate wrapped translations without splitting words.
critique.problems: The horizontal-scrolling row wraps in both English and Arabic, while the final Japanese term leaves a short fragment on a second line. These breaks make the lower rows feel less even.
critique.cause: The 125px English column is still too narrow for the full horizontal-scrolling term; 89px is too narrow for its Arabic equivalent, and 105px is too narrow for the final Japanese term.

critique.good: This is the strongest of the three: the horizontal-scrolling Arabic term and final Japanese term stay on one line, and only the final two rows grow taller. The language columns retain a clear, readable rhythm.
critique.problems: Both long English entries wrap, and the final Arabic entry takes two lines. The English column looks slightly compressed for the table’s entry language.
critique.cause: The 115px English width cannot hold the two longest phrases on one line; the 90px Arabic width accommodates the horizontal-scrolling term but not the longest Arabic entry.

critique.good: The wider English column gives the entry language more breathing room, and all headers and individual words remain intact.
critique.problems: Four consecutive rows are tall, largely because short Arabic phrases wrap. The final Japanese term also wraps, so the gain in English width produces a noticeably looser table without keeping the longest English entries on one line.
critique.cause: Increasing English to 135px leaves only 84px for Arabic and 100px for Japanese. The Arabic column is too narrow for several phrases, while the Japanese column is too narrow for the final term.

review.method: two fresh-context blind reviews; letters shuffled; includes browser auto layout and equal widths as neutral references

ref_equal.why: Chinese, Korean and Arabic fit comfortably, but the narrow English column makes the final term span three lines, and Japanese wraps in two rows.

r2C.why: Extra width in English leaves Arabic so narrow that several short entries wrap, creating tall rows and an uneven balance between languages.

r1B.why: The columns are fairly balanced and most entries fit, though Korean wraps in two rows and Japanese wraps in the final row.

ref_auto.why: The wide English column comes at the expense of the three East Asian columns, where several entries break across lines.

r1C.why: English has ample space, but narrow Chinese, Japanese and Korean columns cause repeated wrapping and fragment the longer entries.

r2B.why: The widths suit the different scripts well: the East Asian entries remain on one line, while the longer English and Arabic entries wrap naturally. Rows remain easy to scan.

raw.unsure: The images are small, so some individual line breaks are difficult to inspect precisely.

r2B.why: The language columns are well balanced: English wraps naturally, the CJK entries remain intact, and only the longest Arabic entry wraps. Rows stay easy to scan.

r1B.why: English and Arabic read comfortably, but the longer Japanese and Korean entries break awkwardly, including a single Korean character on a line.

r2C.why: The wider English column leaves Arabic cramped, causing several Arabic entries to wrap; the longest Japanese entry also breaks. The resulting row heights feel uneven.

ref_equal.why: The narrow English column breaks the last term over three lines, while two Japanese entries wrap. The other columns read comfortably.

ref_auto.why: The wide English column keeps most English text on one line at the expense of cramped CJK columns, where several entries wrap into short fragments.

r1C.why: Several Chinese, Japanese and Korean entries split into short fragments, making the lower rows harder to scan despite comfortable English and Arabic columns.

raw.unsure: The small image size makes individual CJK line endings difficult to inspect, but the differences in wrapping and column balance are clear.

provenance.note: AI visual design judgement; not a human reading study
